_meta.description: Everything that must be answered before a decision can reasonably be made, separated into what the repository already knows, what it does not know, and how the missing piece could be discovered. Each gap names the owner who can actually answer it, because most of these are not research problems: they are facts only the account holder, a seller, or a lawyer can supply.

kinds.Known: Answered from an official source that was read, with the source linked. Listed so a reviewer does not have to re-derive it.
kinds.Unknown - discoverable: Not known yet, but an official source or a reachable party can supply it. The row says exactly where to look.
kinds.Unknown - not discoverable from here: No public official source exists for it in this environment. It needs an account, a legal opinion or a seller. Listed so nobody spends another session looking for it.
kinds.Owner decision: Not a fact at all. A choice only the site owner can make; the row lists the options and what each one commits the site to.

_meta.rule: An Unknown is never closed by inference. It is closed by a named source, a named party's answer, or an explicit owner decision recorded in the Decision log.

questions.question: Is the Associates account enrolled under the supplied Partner Tag, and have the published links been generated and validated in that account?
questions.why_it_matters: Without an account there is no tag, and without a tag no click can be attributed. Every revenue figure the brief asks for is downstream of this single fact.
questions.known: The user supplied `shopnow047c-20` as the selected tracking ID. This session cannot confirm that it is active, belongs to an enrolled Associates account, or has been applied to any Special Link. The three previously reviewed destinations had no visible `tag=` parameter in their 2026-11-16 re-check. Five additional URLs are separately unverified (F-55). The 2026-11-17 reads (data/verification-session-1f4a7a22.json) re-resolved the three links to the same ASINs, again with no tag=; decisions D-01/D-14 (recorded 2026-11-17) publish the tagged Special Links (https://www.amazon.com/dp/<ASIN>?tag=shopnow047c-20) as the outbound hrefs, while the supplied short links stay recorded, unjudged (FLG-003 unresolved). Whether the ID is registered and active is question Q-50.
questions.how_to_discover: In Associates Central, confirm account enrollment and that shopnow047c-20 is the account Partner Tag. Generate or validate one Special Link per intended product; re-resolve each destination and confirm a test click in the authorized reporting workflow before scaling.
questions.answerable_by: The site owner

sources.ref: Operating Agreement (the agreement that creates the account and the tag)

questions.question: Has the account met Amazon's stated prerequisite for API access (at least 10 qualifying sales in the past 30 days)?
questions.why_it_matters: Prices and ratings cannot lawfully be published without an approved Amazon API, and the API has a hard prerequisite. If the prerequisite is not met, no amount of engineering makes a price publishable.
questions.known: Amazon's own Creators API introduction states the prerequisite. The site currently publishes no price or rating (F-02).
questions.how_to_discover: Associates Central shows qualifying sales. The API registration page states whether the account is eligible.
questions.answerable_by: The site owner

questions.known: Both clauses are quoted verbatim in the repository and in flag F-12 and finding A-08. The narrower reading, that the clauses restrict training on Amazon content rather than the writing of original copy, is recorded there with its sources.

questions.question: What counts as success, and over what period?
questions.why_it_matters: The brief asks for click and conversion tracking, but a new site with no traffic will show zeros for months. Without a stated threshold and window there is no way to tell a failing campaign from a site that has not been indexed yet, and the temptation is to fill the emptiness with estimates.
questions.known: The site publishes no attributed click, order or revenue figure because no reporting access is connected. The local tracker records real clicks in the visitor's own browser only.
questions.how_to_discover: Not a discovery question. A reasonable first checkpoint is whether the site is indexed at all; Search Console answers that, and it is the only official source for the site's own impressions.

questions.question: Is a browser-local click log acceptable for this audience, or is a consent notice required first?
questions.why_it_matters: The tracker stores events in localStorage on the visitor's device and sends nothing anywhere. questions.question: Does the cited guidance allow a trend-led topic calendar at all?
questions.why_it_matters: The brief asks for catchy, trendy topics to earn organic traffic. If the guidance this site already cites treats trend-chasing as a warning sign, the topic programme has to be built differently, and that changes D-17 before it is answered.
questions.known: Google's helpful-content guidance lists, among the warning signs of search-engine-first content: 'Are you writing about things simply because they seem trending and not because you'd write about them otherwise for your existing audience?' and 'Are you using extensive automation to produce content on many topics?'. It also asks 'Does your content provide substantial value when compared to other pages in search results?' and 'Are you mainly summarizing what others have to say without adding much value?'. The same page states that SEO is a helpful activity 'when it is applied to people-first content, rather than search engine-first content'. So a trend-led calendar is allowed, but only where each topic is one this site's audience would want and is answered from something the site can source. Recorded as flag F-51.

questions.question: What does the official guidance say about bylines and about disclosing that automation was used?

The helpful-content page adds that trust comes from 'clear sourcing, evidence of the expertise involved, background about the author or the site that publishes it'.

questions.question: Can a redesign move, shrink or restyle the affiliate disclosure?
questions.why_it_matters: Every direction in the design brief places the disclosure differently. If any placement is non-compliant, the direction has to change, not the disclosure.
questions.known: FTC Disclosures 101 states: 'Place it so it's hard to miss. The disclosure should be placed with the endorsement message itself'; 'Disclosures are likely to be missed if they appear only on an ABOUT ME or profile page, at the end of posts or videos, or anywhere that requires a person to click MORE'; and 'Don't mix your disclosure into a group of hashtags or links.' The Associates Operating Agreement Section 5 requires the sentence to be stated 'clearly and prominently', and the Associates help topic adds that a link-level disclosure must be 'clear' - for example '(paid link)', '#ad' or '#CommissionsEarned' - and 'conspicuous ... placed near any affiliate link or product review'. So the disclosure may be restyled and moved within those limits, and may never be collapsed, footnoted or grouped with links.

questions.answerable_by: Already answered by the official sources

questions.question: Do the published articles demonstrate first-hand expertise, and may they?
questions.why_it_matters: Google's guidance asks whether content clearly demonstrates first-hand expertise. If no one has cooked with these appliances, that question cannot honestly be answered yes - and the FTC bars claiming otherwise.
questions.known: No article on the site claims hands-on use, which is correct: FTC Disclosures 101 states 'You can't talk about your experience with a product you haven't tried.' Google's helpful-content guidance asks 'Does your content clearly demonstrate first-hand expertise and a depth of knowledge (for example, expertise that comes from having actually used a product or service, or visiting a place)?' The site therefore answers that question with a different kind of first-hand work: it is the only site that read the listings and recorded what it could not confirm. Whether a human will test the appliances is Q-06 and D-06, both still open.

questions.question: Where may a first-party analytics endpoint run, what are the five event definitions, and what privacy/consent rules govern any reader signup?
questions.why_it_matters: The current localStorage tracker is not shared analytics and cannot report purchases. A server endpoint and reader-capture form would introduce storage and potentially personal data; the site must choose a lawful purpose, consent flow, retention period and deletion path before collection.
questions.known: The public site is generated as static pages. docs/tracker.js makes no network request and stores events only in the visitor browser. There is no reader signup form or Search Console property verification recorded. Associates orders must come from authorized reporting, not inferred from outbound clicks.
questions.how_to_discover: Choose among remaining browser-local-only measurement, a first-party self-hosted endpoint, or an approved managed provider after reviewing hosting, retention, consent, data-subject requests and security. Approve a five-event taxonomy and inspect every payload before enabling collection. Keep reader email separate from analytics; import purchase outcomes only from authorized reports.
questions.answerable_by: The site owner for the purpose, provider, budget and consent choice; an authorized Associates user for order-report access; a privacy professional for applicable legal review.
